title: GPU Architecture Fundamentals
summary: Why a GPU's die looks nothing like a CPU's, and what workloads that shape is actually built for.

slides.markdown:
A **CPU** is built to finish *one* thing as fast as possible: it optimizes **latency**. Deep pipelines, branch prediction, out-of-order execution — all of it exists to shrink the time a single instruction stream takes to complete.

A **GPU** is built to finish *thousands* of things per second: it optimizes **throughput**. Any individual thread may take longer than it would on a CPU, but the chip keeps so many threads in flight that overall work-per-second wins. This one design goal — latency vs throughput — explains almost every structural difference between the two chips.

A CPU core spends most of its die area on **control logic and cache**: branch predictors, reorder buffers, huge multi-level caches — machinery whose whole job is making *one* instruction stream run fast despite dependences and memory stalls.

A GPU core is almost the opposite: it strips control logic down to the minimum and devotes the freed area to raw **ALUs** — thousands of simple arithmetic units. It doesn't need a branch predictor or a reorder buffer per thread because it hides stalls a different way: when one group of threads waits on memory, the scheduler just switches to another group that's ready.

Laying the two dies out to the same scale makes the trade-off visible: a CPU is mostly control and cache with a sliver of ALU; a GPU flips that ratio almost entirely.

![A CPU die area breakdown (mostly control/cache, small ALU area) next to a GPU die area breakdown (mostly ALU area, small control/cache)](assets/cpu-vs-gpu-die-area.svg)

Neither layout is "better" in the abstract — each is the right answer to a different question: minimize the time for *one* task, or maximize the number of tasks finished *per second*.

assets.alt: A CPU die area breakdown (mostly control/cache, small ALU area) next to a GPU die area breakdown (mostly ALU area, small control/cache)

slides.markdown:
GPUs win on workloads that are **massively data-parallel** and **control-flow-uniform**: the same operation applied to millions of independent data elements, with every element following roughly the same path through the code.

Classic examples: shading every pixel on a screen, multiplying huge matrices in a neural network, or running the same physics update across a particle system. In each case there's no meaningful communication between elements while the operation runs, and no element takes a wildly different branch than its neighbors — exactly the profile that lets a chip trade per-thread speed for thread count.

"GPU-shaped" isn't automatic — some problems actively resist it.

| Trait | GPU-friendly | Resists GPUs |
|---|---|---|
| Parallelism | Millions of independent elements | Few independent units of work |
| Branching | Same path for (almost) every element | Heavy, data-dependent branching |
| Communication | Little/none mid-operation | Frequent cross-element dependencies |
| Example | Matrix multiply, pixel shading | A tree traversal with per-node logic, a parser |

A branchy, sequential linked-data-structure algorithm can run on a GPU, but it forfeits most of the throughput advantage — sometimes losing to a plain CPU core.

GPU cores also run at **lower clock speeds** than CPU cores — often ~1.5–2 GHz versus ~4–5 GHz — and each core is far **simpler**: no deep out-of-order machinery, minimal per-core cache, small instruction windows.

This isn't a limitation so much as the same throughput bet again: a simple core uses less power and area per unit of compute, so you can pack thousands of them onto one die. Total throughput comes from **core count × occupancy**, not from any single core's speed — which is exactly backwards from how a CPU chases performance.

slides.sectionTitle: Hiding latency with occupancy, not avoiding it
slides.subTitle: Why a GPU doesn't need a CPU-sized cache
slides.markdown:
A CPU fights memory latency by avoiding it: huge caches, aggressive prefetching, out-of-order execution that finds independent work while a load is in flight. A GPU takes the opposite bet — it **tolerates** latency instead, by keeping so many threads in flight that while one group waits on a slow memory access, the scheduler simply switches to another group that has work ready.

This only works because GPU threads are cheap: thousands of them can be resident at once with their state held entirely in on-chip registers, so switching between them costs nothing (no save/restore, unlike a CPU context switch). The practical consequence: GPU performance depends heavily on **occupancy** — having enough resident threads to always have some ready to run — which is why GPU kernels are written to launch far more threads than there are physical cores, deliberately over-subscribing the hardware.

slides.sectionTitle: Worked example: raw throughput vs what a kernel actually gets
slides.subTitle: Peak FLOPS is a ceiling, not a guarantee
slides.markdown:
A GPU rated at 20 TFLOPS (trillion floating-point ops/second) peak. A kernel that's memory-bound (spends most of its time waiting on memory, not computing) might realize only a fraction of that:

```
peak compute       = 20 TFLOPS
memory bandwidth   = 800 GB/s

kernel needs 1 FLOP per 4 bytes moved (low arithmetic intensity)
achievable FLOPS = memory bandwidth * ops-per-byte
                 = 800e9 bytes/s * 0.25 FLOP/byte
                 = 200 GFLOPS

utilization = 200 GFLOPS / 20,000 GFLOPS = 1%
```

The kernel is nowhere near compute-bound — it's starved by memory bandwidth long before it ever taxes the ALUs. This is the core reason GPU performance tuning is mostly about the *ratio* of compute to memory traffic (arithmetic intensity), not about raw FLOPS at all — a topic worked out fully in [Roofline Model](roofline-model).

slides.sectionTitle: A common trap: assuming more cores always means more speed
slides.subTitle: Amdahl's law still applies to GPUs
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "A GPU with 10,000 cores will always run any parallel workload roughly 10,000x faster than one core."

**Why it's wrong:** every real program has some **serial portion** — setup, a final reduction step, a data-dependent branch that can't be split further — and that portion doesn't speed up no matter how many cores exist. Amdahl's law caps the achievable speedup based on that unavoidable serial fraction, and a GPU's cores are individually much weaker than a CPU's, so the serial portion often runs *slower* on a GPU than it would on a CPU core, not just 'not faster.' A workload that's 95% parallelizable and 5% serial caps out at a 20x speedup no matter how many thousands of GPU cores you throw at the parallel part — which is exactly why real GPU-accelerated pipelines still care about minimizing host-side serial work, not just maximizing core count.
